This period of the PCA also includes development of the proposed approximately 1,400 MW Carbon Capture and Storage (“CCS”)-ready Livingston County Combined Cycle Gas Turbine (“CCGT”) generation facility (“Livingston County project”), with planned commercial operation in 2031, representing the first phase of approximately 2.1 GW of planned new CCS-ready CCGT capacity.

The PCA retires Monroe Power Plant Units 1 and 2 in 2032, removing the final approximately 1.5 GW of coal-fired generation from the Company’s portfolio and completing the Company’s exit from coal, and retires the 76 MW Superior Peaking Station in 2032.

The PCA also includes the proposed approximately 700 MW CCS-ready Monroe County CCGT generation facility (“Monroe County project”), with planned commercial operation in 2032, completing the addition of approximately 2.1 GW of new CCS-ready CCGT capacity.

In addition, the PCA expands the Fermi 2 Nuclear Power Plant through the proposed 177 MW extended power uprate in 2036, increases VPP capacity by approximately 15 MW, and adds approximately 6 MW of CVR/VVO by the end of 2036.

Clair 12-1 and 12-2 peaking units in 2024; converted Belle River Unit 1 from coal to natural gas in 2025 and expects to complete conversion of the Belle River Power Plant to a natural gas peaking resource by the end of 2026; achieved EWR savings exceeding 2.0% in each of 2023, 2024, and 2025; and 2 remains on schedule for the planned Monroe Power Plant retirements.

The Company also completed the required peaker evaluation, which supports the proposed retirement of the Superior Peaking Station in 2032, and conducted the additional modeling, resource adequacy analyses, emerging technology evaluations, and public outreach arising from the 2022 IRP Settlement Agreement and other applicable law. 5.

During the first five years of the planning period, 2027 through 2031, the PCA focuses on satisfying the 2030 RPS and statewide energy storage requirements while implementing the near-term resources necessary to support the phased retirement of the Monroe Power Plant.

The PCA retires Monroe Power Plant Units 3 and 4 in 2028, removing approximately 1.5 GW of coal-fired generation from the Company’s portfolio, while preparing for the retirement of Monroe Power Plant Units 1 and 2 in 2032 and the Company’s resulting exit from coal.

Together, these near-term actions establish the resources and programs needed to maintain reliability through the planned retirement of the remaining Monroe Power Plant Units and the Superior Peaking Station in 2032 and position the Company to satisfy the 2035 RPS and CES requirements and the 2040 CES requirement. 24.

equipment_maker_model: Importantly, in programming their model, the CEOs assumed the addition of natural gas units comparable to what is selected by the Settlement Agreement.

The initial capacity expansion model determined that the best way to serve the demands of our customers would be to add firm dispatchable resources represented by four generic combustion turbines between 2027 and 2029.61 To evaluate the bids, we created a firm dispatchable “hole” between 2027 and 2029 by removing the four generic combustion turbines.

This methodology allows the model to test which bids can meet the identified need for firm dispatchable resources. 60 2019 IRP Order at Order Point 3. 61 The generic combustion turbines modeled in our 2024 IRP have a size of 374 MW.
The model also selects two combustion turbines in 2030. 36 PUBLIC DOCUMENT—NOT-PUBLIC DATA HAS BEEN EXCISED From this point, we ran three different scenarios through the model.

As explained in the IRP filing,67 the Hydrogen Special Study modified the EnCompass model so that hydrogen was the only advanced technology that could be selected, and it allowed hydrogen blending in natural gas firm dispatchable units up to 100 percent beginning in 2030.
Scenario 1, which is the basis for the Settlement Agreement, removed four generic CT units in 2027 and 2028 and allowed the model to select any of the bids provided in Docket 23-212.

The CTs are located at seven different sites and provide peaking capacity meaning they are only typically dispatched a limited number of times a year during peak demand and/or net load conditions.
The CCs are located at five sites and provide intermediate capacity, meaning they tend to operate at higher capacity factors due to better efficiencies and lower dispatch prices when compared to CTs.

Together these plants provide over 4,350 MW of capacity7 and over 29,000 GWh of energy to our customers, which represents 47 percent of the NSP System accredited generating capacity and 65 percent of the system energy.8 This generation is supplemented by several natural gas generating plants located on the 115 kV system in the Twin Cities.
